1:
Who is speaking divides the entry before a word of the psalm is expounded. John Gill answers at once that the petitioner is Christ, not as a divine person but as man in suffering circumstances, offering supplications as a priest whose work was to intercede as well as to sacrifice. C.H. Spurgeon agrees while keeping the double reference: David prayed so, and here his Son and Lord utters the same cry. Keil and Delitzsch hold to the inscription and make the sufferer David himself, unjustly persecuted by Saul, and not, as some have argued, an ideal righteous man. John Calvin leaves the occasion open between the persecution by Saul and the rebellion of Absalom, but reckons that the frequency with which the New Testament applies the psalm, at least seven times, shows it prophetic of Christ, of whom David was an eminent type, and adds that David wrote not so much in his own name as in the name of the whole Church. Adam Clarke breaks with all of them: he supposes it written during the captivity by some Levite divinely inspired, with the psalmist speaking in the person of the captives, and lays down a rule — those portions which the writers of the New Testament apply to our Lord we may apply also, of others we should be careful.

The waters are handled with more agreement. John Wesley glosses them in one word, tribulations. Charles Ellicott calls the sea of troubles a common and obvious figure. Adam Clarke reads the dikes as broken and the flood ready to sweep the captives away. Matthew Henry takes the point of the phrase to be that they have come to the soul: we shall bear up under troubles if we can keep them from our hearts, but when they put us out of the possession of our own souls the case is bad, and the spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, but what shall we do when the spirit is wounded? John Calvin pushes the figure into physiology: a man fallen into an abyss may keep the water out for a time by stopping his mouth and nostrils, but since he cannot live without breathing, suffocation at last compels him to let the water in, and it penetrates to the heart. C.H. Spurgeon makes the same distinction differently — all the sea outside a vessel is less to be feared than what finds its way into the hold.

On the weariness of crying Charles Ellicott prefers calling, and sets beside the verse four English lines on kneeling all night with arms lifted in irresponsive air, dazed with overmuch desiring and blank with the utter agony of prayer. Matthew Henry observes that the throat is dried but the heart is not, the eyes fail but the faith does not. On being hated without a cause he warns that we are apt to use the words to justify our own passion against those who hate us, when they are rather an argument for bearing it patiently. The last clause puzzles everyone. Adam Clarke takes it, with an older commentator, for a proverb of the sort that says those who suffered the wrong pay the costs; the application of it to our Lord he calls very gratuitous. Charles Ellicott renders it what I did not steal I must then restore and thinks it likewise proverbial for harsh treatment, defends the strong word exterminators against the charge of overstatement, and reports a Syriac reading in which the enemies are more numerous than the sufferer’s bones. John Wesley says only that he restored for peace sake. Augustine of Hippo stands apart from the whole discussion, reflecting that what men call felicity is more to be feared than misery, since misery often brings good fruit out of tribulation while felicity corrupts the soul with a perverse security.
5:
The confession of foolishness breaks the christological reading, and four of the five say so. Adam Clarke asks how such words can be attributed to our blessed Lord, however they may be twisted or turned. C.H. Spurgeon grants that David might well say this but not David’s Lord, unless it be taken as an appeal to God about the folly men imputed to him when they said he was mad. Charles Ellicott puts it as a limit rather than a refusal: the verse does not conflict with a true Messianic application, but it is fatal to any view that makes the author not an imperfect type but a prophetic mouthpiece. John Wesley simply lets the speaker be guilty — innocent towards his enemies, but guilty of many sins and follies against God. John Gill alone holds the line and offers three ways of keeping the speaker sinless: the foolishness may be what others accounted such, since he and his followers were reckoned illiterate; or what his enemies charged him with; or the foolishness of his people imputed to him.

The shame that spreads to others is felt by all of them. John Gill thinks of those whose expectation of redemption was almost gone as they walked to Emmaus. John Wesley reads it as the danger of a discouraging example. Adam Clarke hears the taunt from outside, the Gentiles asking how a pure and holy Being can love such a people, and then how God can deal so hardly with those he professes to love; the pious among the captives felt it keenly because the reproach seemed to fall on their God. Charles Ellicott raises it into a principle, calling it a near approach to true churchmanship, the esprit de corps of the Kingdom of Heaven, which makes a sin more heinous because it may harm the brethren; and on the reproaches that fall on the sufferer he notes that had the author been thinking chiefly of his own sin he would have reversed the sentence, so that the reproaches of those who reproach him fell upon God rather than the other way about.

The zeal is variously located. John Gill puts it in the temple and its cleansing, and extends it to the church, the doctrine and the discipline. Adam Clarke makes it a desire to promote God’s glory that has absorbed all other desires. Charles Ellicott allows that the word for house might stand for the congregation, but thinks it more likely a zeal for the restoration or repair of the temple, or rather for its purity and honour. John Wesley says the words truly belong to David and were directed by the Spirit to represent one in whom they were more fully accomplished. Of the fasting and the sackcloth Charles Ellicott says the clause is hardly intelligible as it stands, unless we render that he wept out his soul with fasting, and reports an emendation making it humbled; John Gill admits that we nowhere read of the sackcloth being worn and rests on the mourning it signifies. Adam Clarke closes with the captives at the gate, falsely accused so that they were literally obliged to restore what they had not taken away, and sums up their case: forsaken by friends, scorned by enemies, insulted by inferiors, the scoff of libertines and the song of drunkards, with a deep load of guilt upon the conscience, so that to such a life any death was preferable.
13:
What the acceptable time is depends on where each reader has placed the psalm. Adam Clarke makes it the close of the seventy years that Jeremiah had foretold, so that the captives now pray incessantly for the fulfilment of the promise, and to hear them would itself be the truth of the salvation, showing the promise true. C.H. Spurgeon makes it a division between two courts: it was a time of rejection with man but of acceptance with God, sin ruling on earth while grace reigned in heaven; and he warns that there is to each of us an accepted time, and woe to us if we let it glide away unimproved. Matthew Henry finds it no less acceptable for being a time of affliction, since God will not drive us from him though it is need that drives us to him. Charles Ellicott rearranges the clauses so that the prayer is offered in a time of grace and the hearing asked in the faithfulness of God’s help, and draws a conclusion from it: whatever the sin confessed earlier was, it had not cut the offender off from the blessings of the covenant. John Wesley reads the same appeal as a plea for the salvation God has graciously promised, and John Gill notes that the sufferer answered reviling with prayer rather than reviling, praying for his enemies as well as himself. Matthew Henry draws the practical rule: though we may be jeered for well-doing, we must never be jeered out of it.

The mire, the flood and the pit are read as inward or as outward. John Gill takes the flood for the enemy coming in with his whole company of devils, or else for the wrath of God overwhelming him. Matthew Henry keeps it to the mind: let the waterflood flow upon him but not overflow him, and let him not fall into the gulf of despair, for the pit shutting her mouth would be the end of him; and he observes that the man who gave himself up for lost at the opening of the psalm now has his head above water and is not so weary of crying as he thought. Charles Ellicott alone looks outside the figure. The word rendered pit, he says, is properly a well, and wells were usually covered by a stone, which explains the shutting of its mouth — and then he asks whether this is merely figurative, or whether it preserves the memory of some terrible crime like the one at Cawnpore.

On the lovingkindness pleaded, Adam Clarke works from the words themselves: the first signifies an exuberance of kindness, and the second, which we translate tender mercies, means the affection that mothers bear to their young, and in God there is a multitude of such mercies toward the children of men. Matthew Henry makes the plea itself an argument, since there is in God mercy, tender mercy, and a multitude of it, and if we think well of God under the greatest hardships we need not fear that he will do well for us. John Gill reads the hidden face as what was endured on the cross by one who was God’s servant and about to finish the work given him, and the drawing nigh as the manifestation of favour afterwards; Matthew Henry agrees that the light of God’s countenance is enough to keep a spirit from sinking in the deepest mire of outward trouble. Adam Clarke ends where he began, with the captors growing enraged as they begin to suspect that the redemption of the captives is not impossible after all, and that their own time is short.
19:
The three words heaped together are felt by all of them. John Gill reads them as the sum of what was done to the person and character of the sufferer, the spitting, the buffeting, the veiling of the face, the scourging and the crucifying naked, all of it known to God. C.H. Spurgeon hears in the following clause a whole company brought into court at once, treachery and cunning and counsel and vacillation, Judas and Herod and Caiaphas and Pilate, priests and people and rulers, all seen and all to be judged. Adam Clarke declines to expound: this, he says, is one of the most forcible appeals to mercy and compassion ever made, the language of these two verses is inimitable and the sentiment cannot be mended, and he can devise no comment that would not lessen their effect.

On the broken heart C.H. Spurgeon is at his most literal — there is no hammer like reproach, and our Lord died of a broken heart, slander sufficing to lacerate it till it broke — and he borrows a line about one deserted in his utmost need by those his former bounty fed. John Gill keeps to the heart melted like wax and the soul exceeding sorrowful. Charles Ellicott works on the words instead: full of heaviness is rather I am sick, and both that word and the word rendered pity are favourites with Jeremiah, as are the figures of the verse following, which he takes as evidence of the company the psalm keeps.

The gall and the vinegar divide them. John Gill offers a bitter herb or the gall of some animal. Adam Clarke reads prison rations, food necessary to keep the captives alive but mingled with what made it disgusting, and sour small wines for their drink. Charles Ellicott identifies the word with the poppy, which grows everywhere in Palestine and answers every condition, the familiar rendering having been inherited from the older version; and of the vinegar he observes that sour wine would not be rejected as unpalatable, but was forbidden to Nazarites as a luxury — from which he asks whether the author may himself have been a Nazarite, or whether the whole expression is figurative, setting beside it a line on the banquet where the meats became as wormwood. John Wesley settles the reference the other way, holding that these things were fulfilled metaphorically in David but properly in Christ, whose sufferings were principally intended here.
22:
Whether these are prayers or predictions is the question the whole entry turns on. Adam Clarke says the execrations should be read in the future tense because they are predictive, and not in the imperative mood as though they were the offspring of the psalmist’s resentment: their table shall become a snare, their habitation shall be desolate. John Gill agrees that they are not the effects of a spirit of private revenge, of which there was no appearance in one who prayed for his enemies while they used him so, but prophecies delivered under inspiration; some versions, he notes, render them as futures accordingly, and they are therefore not to be drawn into an example by us. Matthew Henry takes them as prophecies of the destruction of the persecutors, fulfilled about forty years afterwards, and carefully limits their reach: not upon all who had a hand in that death, for some of those repented and found mercy, but upon such as justified it by an obstinate rejection. C.H. Spurgeon concedes a real breach — from this point David and our Lord for a while part company, the severe spirit of the law breathing out imprecations while the tender heart of Jesus offers prayers for his murderers — before allowing that the verses may be viewed as predictions. Charles Ellicott reads them as a recoil rather than an oracle: life had been made bitter by rancour, and the psalmist hurls his curses back couched in the very terms that had risen to his lips to express his own misery. Keil and Delitzsch mark the same place as the turn, the description of the suffering having reached its climax here, where the wrath of the persecuted man flames up.

The table itself is read as exact retribution. John Wesley observes that the punishment in the table answers precisely to the sin of giving gall for meat. C.H. Spurgeon generalises it: it is very easy for the daily provisions of mercy to become temptations to sin, and as birds and beasts are taken by baits for the appetite, so men are snared by their meats and drinks; and since a table serves for conversation, business, counsel and worship as well as feeding, it may become a snare in every one of those uses. Charles Ellicott renders the second clause as a noose set for them in the midst of peace, so that the surroundings of security become the ruin. On the darkened eyes John Gill and John Wesley both understand a judicial blindness of the mind rather than of the body, while Charles Ellicott takes the darkened eyes and the shaking loins together as the ordinary signs of terror and dismay.

The last petitions are handled word by word. Adam Clarke would render the demand about iniquity as a request for its reward, or, since the original signifies perverseness, as a prayer that God treat their perverseness with perverseness and act in judgment as crookedly toward them as they dealt crookedly toward him. Charles Ellicott allows two senses, sin added to sin in the account until the tale is full, or a punishment written down for each wrong. John Gill takes it as a giving up, that they be left alone in sin until the measure is filled, and John Wesley as a giving up to their own lusts. Of the book of the living Adam Clarke says only that they shall be cut off from the life they had forfeited, and John Gill that some understand the catalogue of living saints; Charles Ellicott traces the image to the civil registers, where erasure at first meant no more than that a man was dead or a family extinct, then, since death was held to cut a man off from the covenant, exclusion from the rights of the commonwealth, and at last, as ideas of the end developed, exclusion from the resurrection itself.
29:
C.H. Spurgeon marks the turn: imprecations, prophecies and complaints are ended, and prayer of a milder sort begins, intermingled with bursts of thankful song. Adam Clarke catches the same reversal in the words themselves — I am laid low and full of grief, therefore let thy salvation set me on high; my oppression has laid me low, thy salvation shall make me high. Charles Ellicott reads the lifting up as removal into a secure place out of the reach of enemies. John Gill takes the poverty literally of one born of poor parents, with no certain dwelling place, stripped of his garments and leaving his mother to the care of a disciple. C.H. Spurgeon turns it to the reader: you are trodden down today as the mire of the streets, but you shall ride upon the high places of the earth before long.

The song offered instead of a sacrifice is where the entry turns doctrinal. Matthew Henry finds in it a plain intimation that in the days of the Messiah an end should be put not only to the sacrifices of atonement but to those of praise and acknowledgment which the ceremonial law had instituted, the calves of our lips taking the place of the calves of the stall; and he counts it a great comfort that humble and thankful praises are more pleasing to God than the most costly and pompous sacrifices are or ever were. John Gill uses the verse to confirm the practice of singing in the churches, noting that the sufferer sang praise with his disciples shortly before his death. John Wesley says only that a hearty sacrifice of praise is more grateful to God than the most glorious legal sacrifices. The horns and hoofs divide them. Adam Clarke takes them for the gilded parts of a victim, mentioned because they were the most conspicuous, and supports it from a practice still followed in the east, preferring that to the view that the words mark a full-grown beast. Charles Ellicott reads them as marking at once a clean animal and one of fit age, and John Wesley as marking an age both tender and mature, when the horns bud forth and the hoofs grow hard.

The closing promise settles the date for one of them and not for the others. Adam Clarke says the mention of saving Zion fixes the psalm to the captivity, since there was no Zion belonging to the people in the days of Saul, when those who make David the author suppose it written; the stronghold was taken from the Jebusites only after he came to the throne, and the building of the cities follows the return. He then repeats the rule he laid down at the opening: what evangelists and apostles apply to our Lord we may safely apply, but what others see so clearly in this psalm relative to gospel matters he cannot discern. John Gill reads Zion as the church and the promise as its preservation and its deliverance in the latter day, and the seed of the servants as a succession of converts rather than a natural line. John Wesley keeps both senses at once, a literal inheritance for a long time and a heavenly one for ever. Adam Clarke also takes the poor and the prisoners of the preceding verses at their word, of captives reduced to begging bread from their oppressors and shut up by God’s judgments like culprits in a prison, where Charles Ellicott corrects only the word, reading afflicted for humble, and John Wesley understands those in prison for God’s sake.
